AppAudience.description:
Who an app will sign in.

Only ``PUBLIC`` admits somebody with no standing at all, which is why it is
the one mode a change *to* needs no session sweep: every other value can
only take admission away from somebody who holds it now, and a mode that
refuses the next sign-in while leaving the current one running is not the
control it says it is.

``MEMBERS`` and ``INVITED`` are not ordered against each other. An invited
stranger is not a member, and a member is not necessarily invited, so
"narrower" is not a total order here and nothing tries to make it one --
which is why the sweep asks what is being moved *to* rather than comparing
the two.
AppAudience.title: AppAudience

AppAudienceChangedResponse.description:
An audience change, and the sessions the narrowing ended.

``changed`` is false where the mode was already the one asked for.
``revoked_sessions`` is a count and ``sweep_failed`` says whether it ran,
for the reason a block's are.

audience.description: The mode the app is on now.
audience.title: Audience

changed.description: False where it was already the one asked for.
changed.title: Changed

revoked_sessions.description: How many sessions the narrowing ended. Zero where the sweep failed as well as where there were none -- `sweep_failed` tells those apart, for the reason a block's does.
revoked_sessions.title: Revoked Sessions

sweep_failed.description: Whether ending the sessions the new mode refuses is still owed, which is weaker than any being left running: the sweep is one bulk call, so a failure leaves how many there were unknown -- an app nobody was signed in to reports this too. The mode is committed before the sweep, so the change applied either way. Whatever was signed in ends at the next refresh, and setting the mode again sweeps them.
sweep_failed.title: Sweep Failed

AppAudienceResponse.description:
Who an app signs in, and -- for a caller entitled to it -- who is invited.

``invites`` is null rather than absent for a caller who may read the mode
and not the list, which is a set of email addresses. One shape with a
nullable field rather than two shapes, because a caller cannot discriminate
a union whose members differ only by a key being missing: an empty list and
a withheld list read identically, and "there is nobody invited" is the
opposite answer to "you may not see who is".

says whether it ran. A sweep that failed reports zero and sets the flag,
rather than a null the flag beside it already says more about.

revoked_sessions.title: Revoked Sessions

sweep_failed.description: Whether ending this person's live sessions is still owed. Only a **block** can answer true here: it is written before the sweep, so it applied and how many sessions outlive it is unknown -- the sweep is one bulk call, so a person who was holding none reports this too. An **unblock** lifts the flag after, so a failed sweep deliberately leaves them blocked and changes nothing -- which is a 503 rather than a success, since there is no sense in which the request applied.

AppLogPageResponse.description:
A page of an app's logs, as an object rather than a positional pair.

``logsv2`` answers ``[[...logs...], "cursor"]`` -- the service's tuple,
which no schema can name and which the deployed CLI unpacks by index. This
is the same read with the two halves named, and with a cursor that means
one thing on every provider: *null is the end*.

What it deliberately does not mean is "there is a next page". Proving that
takes a read past the boundary, and neither provider's cursor is one a
lookahead can be built on from here: Loki's is a timestamp this page drains
every tie at (which is also why a page may exceed ``limit``), and Cloud
Logging's is an opaque token it will hand back with an empty page. So a
client loops until the cursor is null and may spend one empty fetch doing
it, which is what ``LokiPage`` records as the cost of a cursor without a
lookahead.

logs.description: The provider's own record shape, named rather than `dict[str, Any]`: it is a TypedDict, so the schema a client generates from this says which fields a log line has.
logs.title: Logs

next_cursor.description: Null proves the walk is over; non-null does not prove a next page. A page that filled exactly to `limit` carries a cursor because neither provider can say without another read -- so a loop ends on a null cursor, which may cost one empty page. `logsv2` is weaker again: its cursor comes back whenever anything did.
next_cursor.title: Next Cursor

AuthenticatedCredentialResponse.description:
The credential ``POST /authenticate/me`` resolved the request from.

``extra="allow"``, which is what makes naming these fields safe: the body
is the identity dataclass encoded whole, so it also carries the per-request
caches that dataclass holds (``_memo`` and friends). Those were never meant
to be published and are not described here -- but dropping them is a wire
change, and this route's whole job is to be the thing a client reads its
own identity from. So the keys that are the answer are named, and whatever
else the encoding carries rides along; the schema says ``additionalProperties``
rather than claiming this is the whole body.

``token_id`` is deliberately not among them: it *is* the bearer credential,
and ``as_response`` holds it out so the caller's own token does not come
back in a body every proxy and access log records.

GenerationResponse.description:
Where a generation got to.

``status`` is ``preparing`` / ``queued`` / ``running`` / ``pushing`` while
the run is live, then ``finished`` / ``failed`` / ``stopped``, or an
``awaiting_*`` -- ``awaiting_question``, ``awaiting_permission``,
``awaiting_plan``, ``awaiting_integration``, ``awaiting_env_vars`` -- for a
run the agent stopped to ask something.

Only ``awaiting_question`` is resolvable here, by creating another
generation on the same ``thread_id`` with the answer as the prompt. A
prompt sent at any other ``awaiting_`` returns the same status: the agent
is instructed that a free-text reply is not a permission grant, and an
integration is connected rather than described.

A plain string, not an enum: a worker one release ahead can send an
``awaiting_`` this client has no name for, and it should read as a parked
run rather than fail to parse.

``detail`` says what the card behind an ``awaiting_`` actually asked, so a
caller can report it and -- for a question -- answer it. It is shaped by
the gate:

- ``awaiting_question``: ``{"questions": [{"question": str, "options": [str]}]}``
- ``awaiting_permission``: ``{"action", "reason", "category", "code"}``
- ``awaiting_plan``: ``{"title": str, "items": [str], "summary": str}``
- ``awaiting_integration``: ``{"integrations": [str]}``
- ``awaiting_env_vars``: ``{"env_vars": [str]}``

An untyped mapping for the same reason ``status`` is a plain string: a gate
added next release carries its own shape, and a client that reads this one
by key keeps working. Null on a run that is not parked, and on a parked one
whose card cannot be read back -- so branch on ``status`` and treat a
present ``detail`` as a bonus, never as the thing that tells you a run is
waiting.
GenerationResponse.title: GenerationResponse

UsageBalanceResult.description:
An org's plan usage this period, as a share of its allowance.

There is no ``allowance_pct``: the allowance is the denominator, so it would
be 100 on every response. ``has_allowance`` is carried because both
percentages are ``"0"`` for an org that was never granted one, which is
otherwise indistinguishable from a plan spent to the last cent.

The last three describe the *next* refill, so a client can render "back to N%
in six hours" without holding a copy of either figure. All three are always
present, so there is one shape to read; the two that describe a refill are
``None`` when there is none, rather than absent.

``refresh_eligible`` is narrower than "will this allowance ever be restored":
it means the org is on the rolling refill in ``cloud.services.refills``. An
Enterprise org, still granted monthly by the billing-period reset, is False
here and the meter's own label is where its boundary is shown -- newly
exposing it under a name that says "refresh" would have a client count down
to a mechanism this field says the org is not on.

``next_refresh_at`` is an absolute UTC timestamp rather than a duration, so a
response that sat in a cache degrades into a countdown a little off rather
than one that is wrong. It is a prediction only while the org keeps coming
back: the refill is granted on the read that notices it is due, so an org
that stays away is refilled when it returns, later than this says.

``next_refresh_pct`` is what the refill is worth against the window it
replaces -- "100" in the ordinary case, because a refill sets the balance
*to* its amount, and less when the window in progress is larger than the plan
it will be replaced by (an admin adjustment). ``None`` when the org holds no
allowance for it to be a share of, the same answer ``amount_pct`` gives a
movement that predates the org's first grant. A share and not the dollars,
like every other figure on this route.

has_allowance.description: Whether the org was granted an allowance at all. Both percentages read `0` for an org that never was, which is otherwise indistinguishable from a plan spent to the last cent.
has_allowance.title: Has Allowance

next_refresh_at.description: When the next refill is due, as an absolute UTC instant rather than a duration, so a cached response degrades into a countdown slightly off rather than one that is wrong. A prediction only while the org keeps coming back: the refill is granted on the read that notices it is due.
next_refresh_at.title: Next Refresh At

next_refresh_pct.description: What that refill is worth against the window it replaces -- `100` ordinarily, since a refill sets the balance *to* its amount, and less where the window in progress is larger than the plan replacing it. Null where the org holds no allowance for it to be a share of.
next_refresh_pct.title: Next Refresh Pct

refresh_eligible.description: Whether the org is on the rolling refill. Narrower than `will this ever be restored` -- an Enterprise org is granted monthly by the billing-period reset and reads false here.
refresh_eligible.title: Refresh Eligible

remaining_pct.description: And what is left of it. There is deliberately no `allowance_pct`: the allowance is the denominator, so it would read 100 on every response.
remaining_pct.title: Remaining Pct

used_pct.description: What this period has spent, as a share of the allowance.

UsageHistoryEntry.description:
One movement against the allowance, as the usage breakdown shows it.

``amount_pct`` is the movement as a share of the grant governing its own
period, unrounded. This range is arbitrary and can span any number of plan
periods, so a single denominator would misquote every row outside the latest
one; and no fixed number of decimals survives every allowance, so a consumer
summing the column would undercount by whatever fell under the cutoff.

Not the allowance at the instant of the charge. An upgrade onto a rolling
tier opens its own window, so its movements are quoted against the plan that
funded them; a within-tier raise still edits the grant in place with no
record of the prior amount, so earlier movements in a raised window are
quoted against the raised figure. The
movements are signed, so summing them gives the remaining share rather than
the used one, and the sum is not meaningful across a plan change.

info.description:
The Reflex Build control plane: apps, deployments, projects, secrets and the organization they belong to.

Requests authenticate with an API token in the `X-API-Token` header. A token is minted from the account settings page, or by `reflex login`.

Every refusal carries `X-Reflex-Error-Code`: a stable token naming the condition, which is what to branch on. The `detail` sentence is prose and three routes word the same condition three ways, so it is not a contract. A refusal nobody has named yet reads `unclassified`. A refusal whose class is coarser than the condition names the condition instead: a provider-account validation that failed one way answers that problem's own code, and one that failed several answers `provider_account_validation` with the full list in the body. The one response without it is a 500 from an error that reached no handler, which is a bug of ours rather than a condition to branch on. Where the condition has a recorded fault, `X-Reflex-Error-Fault` says whose it is -- `transient` is the one that means run it again; an absent header means nobody reached a verdict rather than that it is yours.

**Recent shape changes.** `GET /project/{project_id}/metrics` answers an object where it used to answer the provider's JSON document as a string; a client that decoded the body twice has to stop doing the second decode, and there is no compatible spelling of both. And `GET /apps/{app_id}/environments` renamed `pipelines_allowed` to `front_stage_delete_allowed` -- the old key is published beside the new one and marked deprecated, so a client reading it keeps working until a later release removes it. The three app-auth routes that sweep sessions answer `revoked_sessions` as a count rather than `int | null`: it is zero where the sweep failed as well as where there was nothing to end, and `sweep_failed` is the field that tells those apart. And an unblock that left the person blocked -- because the sweep failed, or because a newer block stands -- is now a 503 or a 409 rather than a 200 whose `blocked` said so. `GET /apps/{app_id}/database` and its connection-string sibling no longer recreate a default database the project has lost: they answer `app_database_needs_reset` (409). `POST /apps/{app_id}/database` recreates it -- as an **empty** database, since the schema and the data went with the one it replaces, so deployed apps read an empty database until something repopulates it. That call is otherwise idempotent for an app that already has a default database and a dev branch. An app provisioned before dev branching has no dev branch and gains one, which changes where writes go rather than what is in them: the builder and the agent's migrations write to the dev branch from then on rather than to the database deploys read.
info.title: Reflex Build API

Add an existing user to an organization, bypassing the invite flow.
Permanently delete an organization and all its projects, members, and billing.

Merge one organization into another, archiving the source.

Members are admitted first, then teams, then projects -- a cross-org move
strips every project member who is not already in the target org, so any
other order would strip everyone the merge is bringing over.

The source is archived rather than deleted: its audit trail carries no org
column and is covered by a global hash chain, and its Stripe customer id is
globally unique, so the row has to survive for either to stay addressable.
A merge that left anything behind archives nothing and says so.

Writes nothing, and reports every blocker, collision and consequence at
once rather than one refusal per attempt. Its ``digest`` is what a merge
request has to echo back: the merge re-assesses under its own locks and
refuses when the picture has moved, so an admin's decision is applied to
what they actually reviewed.

held, adjustments included, goes with it.

The recreated database is **empty** -- the schema and the data went with the one it replaces -- so deployed apps read an empty database until something repopulates it. one already there and only converged it -- which is what ``created`` in the
body says, so the status is the same answer a client that reads only the

**Two things this does beyond converging, and they are not the same.**

It *repairs a missing default database* by creating a new one, which is
the condition `app_database_needs_reset` reports. The new database is
**empty**: the schema and the data went with whatever destroyed the old
one, and this brings back neither. So an app that arrived here through
that 409 comes back working and serving its deployed users an empty
database -- which is the honest result, since the data was already gone
before the caller was sent here, but is not what "recreates it" says on
its own. An app whose default database is intact is untouched by this
half.

branch*. Apps made since get one at provision time: production stays on
the default branch and the builder, the Database tab and the agent's
migrations work on `dev`. An older app has only the default branch, so all
of that reaches the database its deployed users are on -- and this call is
what moves it, whatever brought the caller here. This half changes where
writes go rather than what is in them: the branch is copy-on-write off the
default branch as it stands at that moment, so it takes nothing away from
production. On the repair path that means a copy of the empty database the
other half has just created.

One page at a time. Hosting is metered hourly, so a default 30-day window is
thousands of movements for an org running a handful of apps and a single
response could only ever be the newest few hundred of them. When more remain,

wants the whole window can now reach the end of it.
